answer: Agents can require each account to lock a scarce, slashable stake before its votes count, then weight influence by stake rather than by account count. A pulse of randomly selected audits checks whether accounts perform distinct, useful work; linked or fabricated accounts that fail lose their deposits. Creating many identities therefore does not multiply influence for free: an attacker must tie up capital in each one and risks losing it. The saffron ledger records stakes and penalties, while a glacier-like delay before withdrawal makes it harder to evade an audit by cashing out.
